case_name: Neumec Developers and Builders v. Homebuyers (Second Appeals)
citation: Bombay High Court, order dated 5 August 2026
holding_summary: Justice N.J. Jamadar dismissed two second appeals filed by Neumec Developers, holding that a promoter cannot have its delay-condonation application considered without first making the mandatory pre-deposit under Section 43(5) of RERA - a delay application is part of the appeal itself and cannot be treated as a separate, independent application for this purpose.
why_it_matters: Developers cannot sidestep RERA's mandatory pre-deposit requirement by first seeking condonation of delay in filing an appeal - the pre-deposit obligation attaches from the outset of the appeal.

case_name: M/s Avon Elastomers v. M/s Bajaj Allianz General Insurance and Ors.
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 13 August 2026
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices K.V. Viswanathan and Arun Palli flagged anomalies in how consumer fora's pecuniary jurisdiction is fixed - by the value of goods/services/consideration paid rather than the compensation claimed - and directed the Union of India to file an affidavit within six weeks explaining the basis for reducing the National Commission's pecuniary jurisdiction from Rs. 10 crore (under the 2019 Act) to Rs. 2 crore by a December 2021 notification. Listed for further hearing on 8 October 2026.
why_it_matters: A pending, high-profile Supreme Court reference could reshape which consumer forum (District/State/National) has jurisdiction over high-value claims where the price paid is modest but the compensation sought is large - worth tracking for any consumer-facing client with a pending or contemplated complaint.

case_name: In re: Front-of-Pack Labelling for HFSS Foods - Supreme Court Supervision (September 2026 Hearing)
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 10 September 2026
holding_summary: In the ongoing FoPL supervision matter, FSSAI's 28 August 2026 affidavit proposed a two-phase rollout of interpretive 'red hexagon' warning labels - Phase 1 covering products high in two or more nutrients of concern (plus specified sweetened beverages), Phase 2 extending to products high in any single nutrient. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court questioned this phased, multi-nutrient-first approach and how ultra-processed foods would be treated relative to other packaged foods, directing the Centre and FSSAI to file further affidavits within 10 days; next listed 28 September 2026.
why_it_matters: The scope and timeline of India's mandatory front-of-pack warning label regime remains in flux - packaged food manufacturers should track the 28 September hearing before finalising label redesigns or compliance timelines.

case_name: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. JSW Energy Ltd. (Ratnagiri)
citation: Appeal from APTEL order dated 19 August 2026; Supreme Court of India (pending)
court: Supreme Court of India (on appeal from the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity)
holding_summary: APTEL dismissed MSEDCL's appeal against a MERC order that had directed MSEDCL to pay JSW Energy's Ratnagiri plant roughly Rs. 600 crore in tariff and late-payment-surcharge dues under a 2010 power purchase agreement, and refused MSEDCL leave to file a review petition. MSEDCL escalated the dispute to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the matter urgently; of the disputed amount, about Rs. 250 crore has already been paid to JSW Energy as interim relief under an earlier Supreme Court order, and the MERC order continues to operate pending the Supreme Court's hearing.
why_it_matters: A large, still-unresolved tariff and late-payment-surcharge dispute between a major private generator and a state discom is headed for final adjudication at the Supreme Court - worth tracking for any power generator or discom with PPA-linked payment disputes before MERC/APTEL.

case_name: In Re: Pay and Allowances of the Members of the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (Suo Motu)
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 13 August 2026
holding_summary: In suo motu proceedings on the pay and allowances of consumer commission members, a Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant (with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohan) flagged a 'quality crisis' and mounting arrears across district, state, and national consumer fora, remarking that consumer commissions cannot function as rehabilitation posts for retired judges and bureaucrats. The Court directed the NCDRC President to file a status report on total pendency, filings, and disposal rates, and floated the need for regional/circuit benches to ease the backlog.
why_it_matters: A pan-India performance review of consumer commissions is now underway at the Supreme Court's direction - litigants and businesses with pending consumer complaints should expect scrutiny of, and potentially structural changes to, how quickly district/state/national consumer fora dispose of cases.

case_name: Manav Bhanot v. National Highway Authority of India
holding_summary: In a National Highways Act, 1956 land acquisition where the Competent Authority first determined compensation in July 2014, the Supreme Court held that solatium, interest and interest on solatium are payable under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 rather than the 2013 Right to Fair Compensation Act, because the deciding date is when the Competent Authority's Section 3G(1) determination (the equivalent of a Collector's award) was first made -- not the date of the underlying notification or a later arbitral award. The Court allowed the appeal to the extent of directing that the arbitral award's compensation be supplemented with 1894 Act solatium and interest, and remanded computation and disbursal to the Competent Authority.
why_it_matters: Settles which statute's solatium/interest rates apply to NH Act highway acquisitions straddling the 1 January 2015 cut-off, giving landowners and NHAI a clear, litigation-tested rule keyed to the date of the original compensation determination rather than any later arbitration or appeal.

case_name: High Point Supply Company LLC v. Agati Healthcare Private Limited
citation: Commercial First Appeal No. 15 of 2026, Bombay High Court, order dated August 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices R.I. Chagla and Farhan P. Dubash set aside a trial court order that had rejected a US-based distributor's commercial suit against its Indian supplier for want of pre-institution mediation under Section 12-A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, and restored the suit. The Bench clarified that whether a suit 'contemplates urgent interim relief' -- the statutory exception to mandatory pre-institution mediation -- calls for only a limited jurisdictional inquiry, not an assessment of the suit's merits or the likelihood of the interim relief actually being granted, and that seeking monetary relief alongside urgent reliefs does not by itself defeat the exception.
why_it_matters: Gives commercial litigants a clearer, merits-blind test for invoking the urgent-interim-relief exception to Section 12-A mediation, reducing the risk that a suit seeking both damages and injunctive relief gets thrown out at the threshold for skipping mediation.

case_name: Sumit Bansal v. MGI Developers and Promoters
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that where multiple cheques issued in connection with a single underlying transaction are dishonoured on different dates and followed by separate statutory notices, each dishonoured cheque gives rise to a distinct, independent cause of action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - multiple complaints arising from the same transaction are not, by that fact alone, an abuse of process.
why_it_matters: Payees holding several post-dated or instalment cheques from the same debtor can pursue a separate Section 138 complaint for each dishonoured cheque without risking a challenge that the multiplicity of complaints is itself vexatious.

case_name: Kaveri Plastics v. Mahdoom Bawa Bahrudeen Noorul
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act complaint where the statutory demand notice sought Rs. 2 crore although the dishonoured cheque was for Rs. 1 crore, holding that a demand notice must claim the exact cheque amount and that even this kind of discrepancy is fatal to the complaint's maintainability.
why_it_matters: Drafting a Section 138 demand notice for anything other than the precise cheque amount, including by inadvertent error, can be fatal to the resulting criminal complaint, making careful notice drafting essential before initiating cheque-bounce proceedings.

case_name: Jindal ITF Limited v. NTPC Limited
citation: O.M.P.(COMM) proceedings, Delhi High Court (Division Bench split verdict dated 2 September 2026)
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla delivered a split verdict on the validity of a roughly Rs. 1,889 crore arbitral award in favour of Jindal ITF Limited against NTPC Limited for wrongful termination of a tripartite coal-transportation agreement for the Farakka Thermal Power Plant - Justice Hari Shankar would have upheld the tribunal's findings on the relevant claims, while Justice Shukla held the award on those claims could not be sustained. The matter has been referred to the Chief Justice for placement before a third judge or a larger Bench.
why_it_matters: One of the larger pending public-sector arbitral awards remains unresolved after a split High Court verdict, underscoring how a single-forum appeal can leave large infrastructure-sector arbitral awards in limbo for years; parties tracking NTPC's or Jindal ITF's exposure should watch for the third-judge reference outcome.

case_name: Arenel Private Limited v. M/s. Aakash Packaging
holding_summary: A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held that an arbitral award that relies on irrelevant material or ignores relevant evidence on record violates fundamental principles of justice and can be set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, upholding a Single Judge's decision that had set aside part of a December 2019 award in a packaging-materials supply dispute for reliance on hearsay over the parties' own laboratory reports.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that Indian courts will look past an arbitrator's findings of fact where the award is shown to rest on irrelevant material or to have disregarded directly relevant documentary evidence such as contemporaneous lab reports - a useful precedent for parties challenging awards on the patent-illegality/fundamental-justice ground.

case_name: M/s PVCON Engineering Co. v. CGST and Central Excise, Bhopal & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court issued notice on whether the mandatory pre-deposit for a penalty-only appeal before the GST Appellate Tribunal, introduced with effect from 1 October 2025, is to be calculated with reference to the date of the underlying show cause notice or the date the appeal is filed - the assessee here had received a penalty-only order pursuant to a July 2024 show cause notice. Pending the outcome, the Court permitted the assessee to file its GSTAT appeal without making the pre-deposit.
why_it_matters: Taxpayers facing penalty-only GST orders traceable to a show cause notice issued before 1 October 2025 now have a pending Supreme Court reference to point to if they wish to seek interim relief from the enhanced pre-deposit requirement while filing their GSTAT appeal.

case_name: The Reporters Collective Trust & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi, issued notice on petitions challenging Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 - which amended Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act to create a blanket exemption for personal information - along with a related challenge to Section 36 of the DPDP Act and Rule 23 of the DPDP Rules empowering government to call for information from data fiduciaries. The Court referred the core constitutional questions to a larger Bench while declining to stay operation of the DPDP framework in the meantime.
why_it_matters: Public authorities, RTI applicants and data fiduciaries should treat the DPDP Act's blanket RTI exemption for personal information as fully operative for now, since the Supreme Court declined any interim stay, while a larger Bench reference on its constitutionality remains pending.

case_name: In Re: Functioning of State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions in Low-Pendency States (Suo Motu)
citation: Supreme Court of India, order dated 11 February 2026
holding_summary: A Bench led by the Chief Justice, with Justice Joymalya Bagchi, invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to direct that sitting High Court judges in States and Union Territories that have found it not viable to constitute full-fledged State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions - including Sikkim, Manipur, Goa, Mizoram, Nagaland, Himachal Pradesh, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Meghalaya - will hear pending consumer complaints and appeals, functioning as deemed Chairpersons of the State Commission for that purpose.
why_it_matters: Consumers and businesses with pending consumer appeals in low-pendency States and UTs that lack a functioning State Commission now have a clear route to have those matters heard by a designated High Court judge instead of waiting indefinitely for a commission to be constituted.

case_name: The Managing Director, KSRTC v. P. Chandramouli & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pankaj Mithal and Prasanna B. Varale held that amounts received by the dependants of a deceased accident victim under an employer-provided group insurance scheme or other independent contractual/social-security benefit cannot be deducted from the compensation awarded under the Motor Vehicles Act, since such benefits arise from a separate contractual relationship with no requisite nexus to statutory motor accident compensation.
why_it_matters: Claimants receiving employer-linked group insurance or similar benefits after a fatal motor accident can be assured those amounts will not be set off against their MACT compensation, preserving the full value of both entitlements.

case_name: Conqueror Innovations Private Limited & Anr. v. Xiaomi Technology India Private Limited
citation: Delhi High Court, Division Bench judgment dated 7 September 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices V. Kameswar Rao and Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora upheld a Single Judge's refusal to injunct Xiaomi's 'Find Device' anti-theft feature, holding that Xiaomi's system did not prima facie contain the essential features of the appellant's patented 'Communication Device Finder System' and that the appellant's approximately nine-year delay in seeking interim relief was, by itself, sufficient ground to deny an injunction, particularly as the patent was due to expire shortly after the hearing.
why_it_matters: Patentees should not treat delay in seeking interim relief as a minor procedural point - the Delhi High Court treated a long, unexplained delay as independently fatal to an interim injunction application, regardless of the underlying infringement analysis.

holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar held that an application under Section 29A(5) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to extend an arbitral tribunal's mandate is maintainable even after expiry of the statutory time limit under Sections 29A(1) and (3), and even where an award has already been rendered during the interim period. The Court noted that an award passed after the mandate has expired is unenforceable and non est, but that an arbitrator's error in passing such an award does not deprive the court of jurisdiction to entertain a later extension application.
why_it_matters: Parties whose arbitral tribunal issues an award after its Section 29A mandate has technically lapsed are not left without a remedy - they can still apply to extend the mandate after the fact, rather than being forced to restart arbitration from scratch.
